question:
Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

payload.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
payload.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
payload.holding: The Court held that the multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased, future prospects must be awarded even for fixed/self-employed income based on standardized percentages, and the Court has the power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.
payload.ratio: In motor accident compensation claims under Section 166 of the MV Act, the multiplier must be selected based on the age of the deceased rather than the claimants, future prospects apply to fixed-salary and self-employed individuals, and appellate courts are obligated under Order XLI Rule 33 and the concept of just compensation to correct and enhance inadequate awards.

payload.court: Supreme Court of India
payload.holding: The Supreme Court held that the principles laid down in Swaran Singh's case regarding third-party risks have no application to non-third-party claims such as own-damage claims, and that a fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
payload.ratio: The decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and does not extend to own-damage claims or disputes between the insurer and the insured where no third party is involved.

As noted above, the conceptual difference between third party right and own damage cases has to be
kept in view. Initially, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the license was a fake one. Once it is
established the natural consequences have to flow.
In view of the above analysis the following situations emerge:
1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than
third party risks.
2. Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent
fatality.
3 In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover
the same from the insured.
4. The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to Section 149 of the

The High Courts/Commissions shall now consider the matter afresh in the light of the position in
law as delineated above.
The appeals are allowed as aforesaid with no order as to costs.

National Insurance Company Ltd. and Ors. (2005 (9) SCC 174).
The primary stand of the insurance company is that the person driving the vehicle did not have a
valid driving license. In Swaran Singh's case (supra) the following situations were noted:
(i) the driver had a license but it was fake;

(ii) the driver had no license at all;
(iii) the driver originally had a valid license but it had expired as on the date of the
accident and had not been renewed;
(iv) the license was for a class of vehicles other than that which was the insured
vehicle;
(v) the license was a learner's license.
Category (i) may cover two types of situations. First, the license itself was fake and the second is
where originally that license is fake but there has been a renewal subsequently in accordance with
law.
Chapter II contains Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act relating to licensing of drivers driving the motor
vehicles.
Where the claim relates to own damage claims, it cannot be adjudicated by the insurance company.
But it has to be decided by an other forum i.e. forum created under the Consumer Protection Act,
1985 (in short the 'CP Act'). Before the Tribunal, there were essentially three parties i.e. the insurer,
insured and the claimants. On the contrary, before the consumer forums there were two parties i.e.
owner of the vehicle and the insurer. The claimant does not come in to the picture. Therefore, these
are cases where there is no third party involved.
According to learned counsel for the appellants, in such cases the logic i.e. let the insurer pay and
recover from the insured company does not apply.
As noted above, there is no contractual relation between the third party and the insurer. Because of
the statutory intervention in terms of Section 149, the same becomes operative in essence and
Section 149 provides complete insulation.
In the background of the statutory provisions, one thing is crystal clear i.e. the statute is beneficial
one qua the third party.

the statutory intervention in terms of Section 149, the same becomes operative in essence and
Section 149 provides complete insulation.
In the background of the statutory provisions, one thing is crystal clear i.e. the statute is beneficial
one qua the third party. But that benefit cannot be extended to the owner of the offending vehicle.
The logic of fake license has to be considered differently in respect of third party and in respect of
own damage claims.
It would be appropriate to take note of what was stated in Complete Insulations (P) Ltd. v. New
India Assurance Co. Ltd. (1996 (1) SCC 221). In paras 9 and 10 it was observed as follows:
"9. Section 157 appears in Chapter XI entitled "Insurance of Motor vehicles against
Third Party Risks" and comprises Sections 145 to
164. Section 145 defines certain expressions used in the various provisions of that
Chapter. The expression "Certificate of Insurance"

means a certificate issued by the authorised insurer under Section 147(3). "Policy of Insurance"
includes a certificate of insurance. Section 146(1) posits that "no person shall use except as a
passenger, or cause or allow any other person to use, a motor vehicle in a public place, unless there
is in force in relation to the use of the vehicle by that person or that other person, as the case may be,
a policy of insurance complying with the requirements of this chapter". Of course this provision does
not apply to vehicles owned by the Central or State Government and used for Government purposes
not connected with any commercial enterprise. This provision corresponds to Section 94 of the old
Act. Section 147 provides that the policy of insurance to be issued by the authorized insurer must
insure the specified person or classes of persons against any liability incurred in respect of death of
or bodily injury to any person or damage to any property of a third party as well as against the death
of or bodily injury caused to any passenger of a public service vehicle caused by or arising out of the
use of the vehicle in a public place. This provision is akin to Section 95 of the old Act.

egislative purpose."
More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change
of policy, to formulate a plan of Government. That aim, that policy is not drawn, like nitrogen, out of
the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

The inevitable conclusion therefore is that the decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no
application to own damage cases. The effect of fake license has to be considered in the light of what
has been stated by this Court in New India Assurance Co., Shimla v. Kamla and Ors. (2001 (4) SCC
342). Once the license is a fake one the renewal cannot take away the effect of fake license. It was
observed in Kamla's case (supra) as follows:
"12. As a point of law we have no manner of doubt that a fake licence cannot get its
forgery outfit stripped off merely on account of some officer renewing the same with
or without knowing it to be forged. Section 15 of the Act only empowers any Licensing
Authority to "renew a driving licence issued under the provisions of this Act with
effect from the date of its expiry". No Licensing Authority has the power to renew a
fake licence and, therefore, a renewal if at all made cannot transform a fake licence as
genuine. Any counterfeit document showing that it contains a purported order of a
statutory authority would ever remain counterfeit albeit the fact that other persons
including some statutory authorities would have acted on the document unwittingly
on the assumption that it is genuine".
As noted above, the conceptual difference between third party right and own damage cases has to be
kept in view. Initially, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the license was a fake one.

This applies to both Act policies and contractual policies.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Full Bench directly considered the insurer's liability where a breach of policy conditions (including licence breach) is proved. The ratio is squarely in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench decision that comprehensively analyses the 'pay and recover' principle. It answers every argument the insurer might raise, including the distinction between fundamental and non-fundamental breaches.
supporting.quote: the insurer or Insurance Company is liable to satisfy the award vis-à-vis a third party and is entitled to recover from the insured. This is irrespective of, the policy being an Act policy... or a policy covering other risks by specific contract.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: The Supreme Court held that an insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party has a statutory right to recover from the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The case involved a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab) where the driver had an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable. Our case is stronger on facts (no licence at all), but the principle that third-party rights are paramount applies directly.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court authority that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties overrides policy breaches. The Court explicitly held that it is the 'statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.'
supporting.quote: it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks the appropriate licence/endorsement for the vehicle class, the insurer must indemnify the third party and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had only an LMV licence but was driving a heavy goods vehicle. The court applied the pay-and-recover principle. Our case (no licence at all) is factually stronger for the claimant on the liability point.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the consistent line of authority that third-party claimants are protected regardless of licence defects. The court relied on S.Iyyapan and Swaran Singh.
supporting.quote: the Insurance Company in case of Third Party risks, the Insurance Company has to indemnify the insured. Therefore, we are of the view the Tribunal was right in directing the Appellant-Insurance Company to pay and recover.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the required authorisation/badge, the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation for a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The court directed pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that even where the insurer successfully proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration from third-party liability.
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the claimant... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Even where the driver had no driving licence at all (fundamental breach), the insurer must pay the third-party claimant in the first instance under the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver had no licence whatsoever. The tribunal held it was a fundamental breach but still directed the insurer to pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match in the corpus — a case where the driver had NO licence at all, not merely the wrong class or an expired licence. The tribunal still applied pay-and-recover, protecting the third party.
supporting.quote: the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The case involved expired licences (not no licence at all), but the ratio on statutory liability to third parties is broadly supportive.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and not defeated by licence-related breaches. The court extensively analysed Sections 149(4) and (5) to affirm the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.quote: the liability of the insurance company to satisfy the award passed against third party is a statutory liability and the same is not inhibited by any of the conditions imposed in the policy and any breach of conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: For a deceased aged 42 (between 40-50), future prospects of 25% must be added for self-employed/fixed-salary persons. Multiplier of 14 applies. 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses for 2-3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased in our case is 42 years old, self-employed (or could be treated as such), with 3 dependants. This case applies the Pranay Sethi framework directly.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the quantum framework. The court applied the Sarla Verma multiplier table (age 42 = multiplier 14), 25% future prospects for self-employed aged 40-50, and 1/3rd deduction for 3 dependants.
supporting.quote: An addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years... should be regarded as the necessary method of computation.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh pay-and-recover principle applies ONLY to third-party risks, not to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that if the licence was fake (not merely absent), and if they can somehow characterise this as an 'own damage' or non-third-party context, Swaran Singh does not apply. However, the Supreme Court in this very case clarified that 'in case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' Since our client's claim is a pure third-party death claim, this judgment actually supports us on that distinction.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment expressly states at para 41(3): 'In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised, to recover the same from the insured.' Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's claim is a third-party claim (death of a pedestrian/other road user caused by the insured truck). The insurer cannot use Laxmi Narain Dhut to avoid third-party liability — the case itself draws the distinction that preserves third-party protection.
adverse.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without any licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured/owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite the finding that 'no liability can be fastened upon Insurance Company' to argue they should be exonerated entirely. However, the same tribunal went on to apply pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant. The insurer will selectively quote the exoneration language while ignoring the pay-and-recover direction.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The same judgment that found a fundamental breach also directed the insurer to pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner. The tribunal expressly held: 'the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover.' The insurer's argument collapses on reading the full judgment.
adverse.quote: it is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: Absence of a special endorsement on the driving licence (for hazardous goods transport) constitutes a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that a licence defect (here, no licence at all) is a breach. But the case actually supports pay-and-recover, not exoneration. Low risk.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court expressly held: 'the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.' This supports our position.
adverse.quote: the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

priority_arguments: The insurer's liability to third parties is STATUTORY under Section 149 of the MV Act, not contractual. The claimant (a third-party road user) cannot be made to suffer for the insured's breach.

The consistent line of Supreme Court and High Court authority (Satto, Yallavva, S.Iyyapan, Chennamma, Sunil Shreesail Killiket) establishes that even where the driver had NO licence at all, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant first and may recover from the insured owner/driver.

The burden of proving the licence breach is on the insurer. The insurer must prove (a) that the driver had no licence, AND (b) that the owner had knowledge of or connived in the breach (the 'twin test' from Swaran Singh). If the owner was a transport company that employed the driver, the insurer must show the company failed to exercise due diligence.

Quantum: Deceased aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). Under Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma: 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 40-50), multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction. Conventional heads: Rs 19,965 (loss of estate) + Rs 19,965 (funeral) + Rs 1,59,720 (spousal + parental consortium for 3 claimants). Total ~Rs 51 lakh.
Interest: Claimant is entitled to interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of the claim petition until realisation.

The insurer cannot avoid liability by arguing the policy is 'void' — Section 149(2)(b) (policy void for non-disclosure) is a separate ground that requires proof of material non-disclosure by the insured, not merely an unlicensed driver. The insurer's defence falls under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) (breach of condition), which triggers pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of petition
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 x 12 = Rs 4,20,000 annual. Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42 per Pranay Sethi) = Rs 5,25,000. Deduct 1/3rd for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma) = Rs 3,50,000. Apply multiplier 14 (age 42 per Sarla Verma table) = Rs 49,00,000. Add conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 1,59,720 (Rs 53,240 x 3 claimants per Magma General/Satinder Kaur) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. Range reflects potential dispute on employment status (self-employed vs permanent) affecting future prospects percentage.
risks: The insurer may argue that the driver having NO licence at all is a more serious breach than having the wrong class of licence, and may seek to distinguish cases like S.Iyyapan (where the driver had an LMV licence). However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this — the driver had no licence and the tribunal still applied pay-and-recover.

The insurer may argue that the transport company owner was complicit (the 'twin test' from Swaran Singh). If the owner knew the driver had no licence, the insurer may argue this is a conscious breach. However, even conscious breach triggers pay-and-recover, not exoneration, as held in Yallavva (doc_025).

The insurer may challenge the income of Rs 35,000/month if not supported by documentary proof. The claimant should gather salary slips, bank statements, IT returns, or any other proof of the deceased's income.
If the deceased was a daily-wage earner or in informal employment, the tribunal may assess notional income lower than Rs 35,000. The claimant should lead best available evidence of income.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 of the MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the entire compensation with interest, with liberty to recover from the insured owner/driver. Alternatively, if the insurer is exonerated, seek a direction that the insurer pay-and-recover. Also implead the truck owner and driver as respondents.

caveats: The corpus does not contain the landmark Supreme Court judgment in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297, which is the foundational authority for the pay-and-recover principle. Multiple judgments in the corpus (Satto, Yallavva, Chennamma, Vijayakumar) cite and apply Swaran Singh. Counsel should independently read Swaran Singh.

The corpus does not contain Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680 (Constitution Bench on quantum). The quantum framework in this report relies on Surendra Singh (doc_019) which applies Pranay Sethi, and on the compute_quantum tool which implements the Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma framework.

The corpus does not contain Magma General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Nanu Ram (2018) 18 SCC 130 or United India Insurance Co. v. Satinder Kaur (2020) 11 SCC 419 on consortium for multiple claimants. The conventional heads calculation relies on these authorities as applied by the compute_quantum tool.

doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) is a Tribunal-level decision, not a High Court or Supreme Court judgment. While factually on point, its precedential value is limited. However, it correctly applies Supreme Court principles (Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba, Shamanna v. Oriental Insurance) which are binding.

doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is a Supreme Court judgment that the insurer will certainly cite. However, as analysed above, it supports the claimant on the third-party point. Counsel should be prepared to distinguish it on facts if the insurer tries to stretch it.

args.question: Motor accident claim for death of spouse (42-year-old male, Rs 35,000/month, wife + 2 minor children). Commercial truck driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void. Research supporting and adverse precedents, and strategy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory under Section 149 of the MV Act. Even if the insurer proves a breach of policy conditions (including an invalid driving licence), it must pay the third-party claimant first and may then recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver had no valid licence; the court held the insurer statutorily liable to pay the third-party award with recovery rights against the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority for the proposition that National Insurance Co. cannot escape liability to Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. The insurer must pay first, then recover from the truck owner. The claimant is a third party and cannot be made to suffer.
supporting.quote: the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be, as ordered by the Claims Tribunal or the Court.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: A Full Bench of the Karnataka High Court held that even when a breach under Section 149(2) (including invalid licence) is successfully proved, the insurer must satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured. This applies to both Act policies and contractual policies.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Full Bench directly considered the insurer's liability where a breach of policy conditions (including licence breach) is proved. The ratio is squarely in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench decision that comprehensively analyses the 'pay and recover' principle. It answers every argument the insurer might raise, including the distinction between fundamental and non-fundamental breaches.
supporting.quote: the insurer or Insurance Company is liable to satisfy the award vis-à-vis a third party and is entitled to recover from the insured. This is irrespective of, the policy being an Act policy... or a policy covering other risks by specific contract.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: The Supreme Court held that an insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party has a statutory right to recover from the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The case involved a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab) where the driver had an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable. Our case is stronger on facts (no licence at all), but the principle that third-party rights are paramount applies directly.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court authority that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties overrides policy breaches. The Court explicitly held that it is the 'statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.'
supporting.quote: it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Even where the driver had no driving licence at all (fundamental breach), the insurer must pay the third-party claimant in the first instance under the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver had no licence whatsoever. The tribunal held it was a fundamental breach but still directed the insurer to pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match in the corpus — a case where the driver had NO licence at all, not merely the wrong class or an expired licence. The tribunal still applied pay-and-recover, protecting the third party.
supporting.quote: the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks the appropriate licence/endorsement for the vehicle class, the insurer must indemnify the third party and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had only an LMV licence but was driving a heavy goods vehicle. The court applied the pay-and-recover principle. Our case (no licence at all) is factually stronger for the claimant on the liability point.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the consistent line of authority that third-party claimants are protected regardless of licence defects. The court relied on S.Iyyapan and Swaran Singh.
supporting.quote: the Insurance Company in case of Third Party risks, the Insurance Company has to indemnify the insured. Therefore, we are of the view the Tribunal was right in directing the Appellant-Insurance Company to pay and recover.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the required authorisation/badge, the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation for a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The court directed pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that even where the insurer successfully proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration from third-party liability.
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the claimant... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The case involved expired licences (not no licence at all), but the ratio on statutory liability to third parties is broadly supportive.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and not defeated by licence-related breaches. The court extensively analysed Sections 149(4) and (5) to affirm the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.quote: the liability of the insurance company to satisfy the award passed against third party is a statutory liability and the same is not inhibited by any of the conditions imposed in the policy and any breach of conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: For a deceased aged 42 (between 40-50), future prospects of 25% must be added for self-employed/fixed-salary persons. Multiplier of 14 applies. 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses for 2-3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased in our case is 42 years old, self-employed (or could be treated as such), with 3 dependants. This case applies the Pranay Sethi framework directly.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the quantum framework. The court applied the Sarla Verma multiplier table (age 42 = multiplier 14), 25% future prospects for self-employed aged 40-50, and 1/3rd deduction for 3 dependants.
supporting.quote: An addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years... should be regarded as the necessary method of computation.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence had expired and was renewed after the accident, the driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date. However, the insurer was directed to pay the third-party claimant and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer proved the licence was invalid (expired). The court still applied pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant. This supports our position that even proven breach leads to pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that even where the insurer successfully proves the licence defect, the third-party claimant is protected by the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh pay-and-recover principle applies ONLY to third-party risks, not to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that if the licence was fake (not merely absent), the pay-and-recover principle does not apply. However, the Supreme Court in this very case clarified that 'in case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' Since our client's claim is a pure third-party death claim, this judgment actually supports us on that distinction.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment expressly states at para 41(3): 'In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised, to recover the same from the insured.' Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's claim is a third-party claim (death of a pedestrian/other road user caused by the insured truck). The insurer cannot use Laxmi Narain Dhut to avoid third-party liability — the case itself draws the distinction that preserves third-party protection.
adverse.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence can constitute contributory negligence, and the tribunal deducted 50% of compensation on that basis where the injured claimant himself was driving without a licence.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that the deceased (if he was the driver of the other vehicle involved) was driving without a licence and therefore contributed to the accident. However, in our case the deceased was NOT the driver — he was a third-party victim (pedestrian/occupant of another vehicle) killed by the truck. Contributory negligence does not arise on these facts.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved the injured claimant himself driving without a licence and without a helmet — he was the author of his own injury. In our case, the deceased was a third-party victim, not the driver of the offending vehicle. The deceased's lack of a licence (if any) is irrelevant to the accident. Contributory negligence requires a causal connection between the deceased's conduct and the accident, which is absent here.
adverse.quote: he did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and the Tribunal cannot invoke 'pay and recover' to compel the insurer to satisfy the award.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that 'pay and recover' cannot be ordered in certain cases. However, this case is about passengers in a private vehicle used for hire — a fundamentally different category from a third-party road user killed by a commercial truck. The ratio is expressly limited to persons who are not 'third parties' under the Act.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case deals with passengers in a private vehicle hired for reward — persons who are NOT 'third parties' under Section 147. Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's husband was a third-party road user (pedestrian/other vehicle occupant) killed by the insured truck. He is squarely a 'third party' under the Act. The court in Sukumarbai itself distinguished third-party claims from passenger claims. This case does not apply.
adverse.quote: when the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as 'third party'; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of 'pay and recover' in this case.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where passengers carried in a goods vehicle or tractor are gratuitous passengers whose risk is neither covered by statute nor by the insurance policy, the Claims Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct the insurance company to first pay the compensation and then recover it from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover cannot be ordered where the risk is not statutorily covered. However, this case is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a category the Supreme Court has held is NOT covered by the statutory insurance requirement. Our client's deceased was a third-party road user, whose risk IS statutorily required to be covered under Section 147.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is expressly limited to gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — persons whose risk is not statutorily required to be insured under Section 147. Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's husband was a third-party road user (not a passenger in the goods vehicle). His risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147. The court in Minor Mahesh Kanubhai itself distinguished third-party claims from gratuitous passenger claims. The ratio does not apply.
adverse.quote: in cases involving third parties, where the Supreme Court, after finding the insurance company not liable, has directed the insurance company to first pay the awarded amount and then recover the same from the insured/owner, such powers are relatable to sub-section (4) and (5) of the Act.

adverse.title: Shivlal And Ors. Etc. vs Smt. Rukmabai And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is not liable to pay compensation for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that they are not liable for certain categories of claimants. However, this case is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a completely different category from a third-party road user.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case deals with a gratuitous passenger in a tractor (goods vehicle) — a person whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered. Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's husband was a third-party road user killed by the truck. He is not a passenger in the goods vehicle. The ratio is entirely inapplicable.
adverse.quote: the insurer is not liable to pay compensation for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Ellappa ... 1St
adverse.principle: The insurance company has no statutory liability to pay compensation to passengers travelling in a goods vehicle, but appellate courts retain discretion to apply 'pay and recover' depending on facts.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is discretionary, not automatic. However, this case is about passengers in goods vehicles, not third-party road users. The court actually applied pay-and-recover despite finding no statutory liability.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns passengers in goods vehicles (gratuitous passengers). The court held the insurer had no statutory liability but still applied pay-and-recover considering the claimants' circumstances. Our case is stronger — the deceased was a third-party road user whose risk IS statutorily covered. Pay-and-recover is not discretionary here; it is mandated by Section 149(4).
adverse.quote: The insurance company is not statutorily liable to cover passengers travelling in a goods vehicle, but considering the prolonged litigation and status of the claimants, a 'pay and recover' order is issued against the insurance company.

adverse.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
adverse.principle: Where a tractor was used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer was absolved from liability.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that breach of policy conditions can lead to full exoneration. However, this case is about a use-of-vehicle breach (agricultural vs non-agricultural use), not a licence breach. The legal framework for licence breaches under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) is different.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involves a breach of a use restriction (agricultural use only) — a policy condition that goes to the scope of the risk undertaken. Licence breaches under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) are governed by a different legal framework (Swaran Singh, Satto, Yallavva) which mandates pay-and-recover for third-party claims. The two categories of breach are treated differently.
adverse.quote: the insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation and the owner of the tractor will have to pay the compensation.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that if any claimant was not dependent on the deceased, their claim for loss of dependency should be rejected. However, in our case, the wife and two minor children (aged 8 and 12) are clearly dependants. This case does not apply.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a major son who was gainfully employed and not dependent on the deceased. Mrs. Lakshmi Devi is the widow, and the two children are minors (8 and 12) — all clearly dependants. The ratio actually supports our position by negative implication: genuine dependants are entitled to loss of dependency.
adverse.quote: a legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'

priority_arguments: The insurer's liability to third parties is STATUTORY under Section 149 of the MV Act, not contractual. The claimant (a third-party road user) cannot be made to suffer for the insured's breach.

The consistent line of Supreme Court and High Court authority (Satto, Yallavva, S.Iyyapan, Chennamma, Sunil Shreesail Killiket) establishes that even where the driver had NO licence at all, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant first and may recover from the insured owner/driver.

The burden of proving the licence breach is on the insurer. The insurer must prove (a) that the driver had no licence, AND (b) that the owner had knowledge of or connived in the breach (the 'twin test' from Swaran Singh). If the owner was a transport company that employed the driver, the insurer must show the company failed to exercise due diligence.

Quantum: Deceased aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). Under Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma: 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 40-50), multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction. Conventional heads: Rs 19,965 (loss of estate) + Rs 19,965 (funeral) + Rs 1,59,720 (spousal + parental consortium for 3 claimants). Total ~Rs 51 lakh.
Interest: Claimant is entitled to interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of the claim petition until realisation.

The insurer cannot avoid liability by arguing the policy is 'void' — Section 149(2)(b) (policy void for non-disclosure) is a separate ground that requires proof of material non-disclosure by the insured, not merely an unlicensed driver. The insurer's defence falls under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) (breach of condition), which triggers pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of petition
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 x 12 = Rs 4,20,000 annual. Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42 per Pranay Sethi) = Rs 5,25,000. Deduct 1/3rd for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma) = Rs 3,50,000. Apply multiplier 14 (age 42 per Sarla Verma table) = Rs 49,00,000. Add conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 1,59,720 (Rs 53,240 x 3 claimants per Magma General/Satinder Kaur) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. Range reflects potential dispute on employment status (self-employed vs permanent) affecting future prospects percentage.
risks: The insurer may argue that the driver having NO licence at all is a more serious breach than having the wrong class of licence, and may seek to distinguish cases like S.Iyyapan (where the driver had an LMV licence). However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this — the driver had no licence and the tribunal still applied pay-and-recover.

The insurer may argue that the transport company owner was complicit (the 'twin test' from Swaran Singh). If the owner knew the driver had no licence, the insurer may argue this is a conscious breach. However, even conscious breach triggers pay-and-recover, not exoneration, as held in Yallavva (doc_025).

The insurer may challenge the income of Rs 35,000/month if not supported by documentary proof. The claimant should gather salary slips, bank statements, IT returns, or any other proof of the deceased's income.
If the deceased was in informal employment, the tribunal may assess notional income lower than Rs 35,000. The claimant should lead best available evidence of income.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 of the MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the entire compensation with interest, with liberty to recover from the insured owner/driver. Alternatively, if the insurer is exonerated, seek a direction that the insurer pay-and-recover. Also implead the truck owner and driver as respondents.

caveats: The corpus does not contain the landmark Supreme Court judgment in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297, which is the foundational authority for the pay-and-recover principle. Multiple judgments in the corpus (Satto, Yallavva, Chennamma, Vijayakumar) cite and apply Swaran Singh. Counsel should independently read Swaran Singh.

The corpus does not contain Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680 (Constitution Bench on quantum). The quantum framework in this report relies on Surendra Singh (doc_019) which applies Pranay Sethi, and on the compute_quantum tool which implements the Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma framework.

The corpus does not contain Magma General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Nanu Ram (2018) 18 SCC 130 or United India Insurance Co. v. Satinder Kaur (2020) 11 SCC 419 on consortium for multiple claimants. The conventional heads calculation relies on these authorities as applied by the compute_quantum tool.

doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) is a Tribunal-level decision, not a High Court or Supreme Court judgment. While factually on point, its precedential value is limited. However, it correctly applies Supreme Court principles (Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba, Shamanna v. Oriental Insurance) which are binding.

doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is a Supreme Court judgment that the insurer will certainly cite. However, as analysed in adverse section, it supports the claimant on the third-party point. Counsel should be prepared to distinguish it on facts if the insurer tries to stretch it.

doc_016 (Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State Of H.P) and doc_017 (Sanjay vs State Of Haryana) are criminal revision cases about rash driving convictions under IPC. They do not address civil liability, insurance, or licence breach issues and are irrelevant to this claim.
doc_038 (M/S Crown Consultants (P) Ltd. vs The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd.) is a consumer dispute about late claim filing — entirely unrelated to motor accident third-party claims.

doc_051 (Sh. Yashpal Chaudhrani & Ors. vs State) and doc_054 (Chinnasamy vs K.Viswanathan) are criminal quashing and specific performance cases respectively — completely unrelated to motor accident insurance.

doc_006 (National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others) focuses on contributory negligence and quantum enhancement. It does not address insurer liability for licence breach and is not adverse on the liability issue.

1. These are the two First Appeals from Order under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988
directed against the judgment and award dated 7th August, 2001, passed by Motor Accident Claims
Tribunal/II Additional District Judge, Faizabad, directing the appellant-Assurance Company to pay
a sum ' of Rs. 16,09,000, as compensation with interest @ 9% per annum from the date of filing of
the petition till the date of actual payment.
2. F.A.F.O. No. 510 of 2001 has been filed by the New India Assurance Company Ltd. challenging
the legality and correctness of the award directing the payment of the aforesaid sum, whereas
F.A.F.O. No. 509 of 2001 has been filed by the claimants for enhancement of the amount of
compensation.
3. Both the appeals having arisen out of the same judgment and award and common questions of
law and fact being involved, we propose to dispose of both the appeals by this common judgment.
4. Briefly stated facts giving rise to these appeals are that Dr. Kamlesh Kumar, who was an Eye
Surgeon, aged about 43 years, while moving on his Scooter No. U.P. 42/1395 was knocked down by
a Jeep, bearing registration No. P. 42-A 0174. He sustained serious injuries. A vehicle belonging to
the Health Department of the district, was coming from the opposite side, wherefrom Dr. Kamlesh

priority_arguments: The insurer's liability to third parties is STATUTORY under Section 149 of the MV Act, not contractual. The claimant (a third-party road user) cannot be made to suffer for the insured's breach.

The consistent line of Supreme Court and High Court authority (Satto, Yallavva, S.Iyyapan, Chennamma, Sunil Shreesail Killiket) establishes that even where the driver had NO licence at all, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant first and may recover from the insured owner/driver.

The burden of proving the licence breach is on the insurer. The insurer must prove (a) that the driver had no licence, AND (b) that the owner had knowledge of or connived in the breach (the 'twin test' from Swaran Singh). If the owner was a transport company that employed the driver, the insurer must show the company failed to exercise due diligence.

Quantum: Deceased aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). Under Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma: 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 40-50), multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction. Conventional heads: Rs 19,965 (loss of estate) + Rs 19,965 (funeral) + Rs 1,59,720 (spousal + parental consortium for 3 claimants). Total ~Rs 51 lakh.
Interest: Claimant is entitled to interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of the claim petition until realisation.

The insurer cannot avoid liability by arguing the policy is 'void' — Section 149(2)(b) (policy void for non-disclosure) is a separate ground that requires proof of material non-disclosure by the insured, not merely an unlicensed driver. The insurer's defence falls under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) (breach of condition), which triggers pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of petition
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 x 12 = Rs 4,20,000 annual. Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42 per Pranay Sethi) = Rs 5,25,000. Deduct 1/3rd for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma) = Rs 3,50,000. Apply multiplier 14 (age 42 per Sarla Verma table) = Rs 49,00,000. Add conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 1,59,720 (Rs 53,240 x 3 claimants per Magma General/Satinder Kaur) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. Range reflects potential dispute on employment status (self-employed vs permanent) affecting future prospects percentage.
risks: The insurer may argue that the driver having NO licence at all is a more serious breach than having the wrong class of licence, and may seek to distinguish cases like S.Iyyapan (where the driver had an LMV licence). However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this — the driver had no licence and the tribunal still applied pay-and-recover.

The insurer may argue that the transport company owner was complicit (the 'twin test' from Swaran Singh). If the owner knew the driver had no licence, the insurer may argue this is a conscious breach. However, even conscious breach triggers pay-and-recover, not exoneration, as held in Yallavva (doc_025).

The insurer may challenge the income of Rs 35,000/month if not supported by documentary proof. The claimant should gather salary slips, bank statements, IT returns, or any other proof of the deceased's income.
If the deceased was in informal employment, the tribunal may assess notional income lower than Rs 35,000. The claimant should lead best available evidence of income.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 of the MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the entire compensation with interest, with liberty to recover from the insured owner/driver. Alternatively, if the insurer is exonerated, seek a direction that the insurer pay-and-recover. Also implead the truck owner and driver as respondents.

caveats: The corpus does not contain the landmark Supreme Court judgment in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297, which is the foundational authority for the pay-and-recover principle. Multiple judgments in the corpus (Satto, Yallavva, Chennamma, Vijayakumar) cite and apply Swaran Singh. Counsel should independently read Swaran Singh.

The corpus does not contain Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680 (Constitution Bench on quantum). The quantum framework in this report relies on Surendra Singh (doc_019) which applies Pranay Sethi, and on the compute_quantum tool which implements the Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma framework.

The corpus does not contain Magma General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Nanu Ram (2018) 18 SCC 130 or United India Insurance Co. v. Satinder Kaur (2020) 11 SCC 419 on consortium for multiple claimants. The conventional heads calculation relies on these authorities as applied by the compute_quantum tool.

doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) is a Tribunal-level decision, not a High Court or Supreme Court judgment. While factually on point, its precedential value is limited. However, it correctly applies Supreme Court principles (Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba, Shamanna v. Oriental Insurance) which are binding.

doc_028 (Sukumarbai), doc_029 (Minor Mahesh Kanubhai), doc_014 (Shivlal), and doc_026 (Ellappa) are all about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a category the Supreme Court has held is NOT covered by the statutory insurance requirement. They are entirely inapplicable to our case where the deceased was a third-party road user, not a passenger in the offending vehicle.

doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) is about a tractor used for non-agricultural purposes — a use-of-vehicle breach, not a licence breach. The legal framework for licence breaches under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) is different and governed by Swaran Singh/Satto/Yallavva which mandate pay-and-recover.

doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) is about a non-dependent legal representative (major employed son) not being entitled to loss of dependency. Our claimants are a widow and two minor children — all clearly dependants. This case is irrelevant.
doc_016 and doc_017 are criminal revision cases about rash driving convictions under IPC. They do not address civil liability, insurance, or licence breach issues and are irrelevant.

doc_023 (Suman Lata) is about reduction of interest rate from 9% to 7.5% and the insurer's inability to challenge quantum without Section 170 permission. It does not address licence breach or insurer liability.
doc_038 (Crown Consultants) is a consumer dispute about late claim filing — entirely unrelated to motor accident third-party claims.
doc_051 (Yashpal Chaudhrani) and doc_054 (Chinnasamy) are criminal quashing and specific performance cases respectively — completely unrelated to motor accident insurance.
doc_006 (Meena) focuses on contributory negligence and quantum enhancement. It does not address insurer liability for licence breach and is not adverse on the liability issue.

However, in our case the deceased was NOT the driver — he was a third-party victim killed by the truck. Contributory negligence does not arise on these facts.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved the injured claimant himself driving without a licence and without a helmet — he was the author of his own injury. In our case, the deceased was a third-party victim, not the driver of the offending vehicle. The deceased's lack of a licence (if any) is irrelevant to the accident. Contributory negligence requires a causal connection between the deceased's conduct and the accident, which is absent here.
adverse.quote: he did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

priority_arguments: The insurer's liability to third parties is STATUTORY under Section 149 of the MV Act, not contractual. The claimant (a third-party road user) cannot be made to suffer for the insured's breach.

The consistent line of Supreme Court and High Court authority (Satto, Yallavva, S.Iyyapan, Chennamma, Sunil Shreesail Killiket) establishes that even where the driver had NO licence at all, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant first and may recover from the insured owner/driver.

The burden of proving the licence breach is on the insurer. The insurer must prove (a) that the driver had no licence, AND (b) that the owner had knowledge of or connived in the breach (the 'twin test' from Swaran Singh). If the owner was a transport company that employed the driver, the insurer must show the company failed to exercise due diligence.

Quantum: Deceased aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). Under Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma: 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 40-50), multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction. Conventional heads: Rs 19,965 (loss of estate) + Rs 19,965 (funeral) + Rs 1,59,720 (spousal + parental consortium for 3 claimants). Total ~Rs 51 lakh.
Interest: Claimant is entitled to interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of the claim petition until realisation.

The insurer cannot avoid liability by arguing the policy is 'void' — Section 149(2)(b) (policy void for non-disclosure) is a separate ground that requires proof of material non-disclosure by the insured, not merely an unlicensed driver. The insurer's defence falls under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) (breach of condition), which triggers pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of petition
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 x 12 = Rs 4,20,000 annual. Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42 per Pranay Sethi) = Rs 5,25,000. Deduct 1/3rd for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma) = Rs 3,50,000. Apply multiplier 14 (age 42 per Sarla Verma table) = Rs 49,00,000. Add conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 1,59,720 (Rs 53,240 x 3 claimants per Magma General/Satinder Kaur) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. Range reflects potential dispute on employment status (self-employed vs permanent) affecting future prospects percentage.
risks: The insurer may argue that the driver having NO licence at all is a more serious breach than having the wrong class of licence, and may seek to distinguish cases like S.Iyyapan (where the driver had an LMV licence). However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this — the driver had no licence and the tribunal still applied pay-and-recover.

The insurer may argue that the transport company owner was complicit (the 'twin test' from Swaran Singh). If the owner knew the driver had no licence, the insurer may argue this is a conscious breach. However, even conscious breach triggers pay-and-recover, not exoneration, as held in Yallavva (doc_025).

The insurer may challenge the income of Rs 35,000/month if not supported by documentary proof. The claimant should gather salary slips, bank statements, IT returns, or any other proof of the deceased's income.
If the deceased was in informal employment, the tribunal may assess notional income lower than Rs 35,000. The claimant should lead best available evidence of income.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 of the MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the entire compensation with interest, with liberty to recover from the insured owner/driver. Alternatively, if the insurer is exonerated, seek a direction that the insurer pay-and-recover. Also implead the truck owner and driver as respondents.

caveats: The corpus does not contain the landmark Supreme Court judgment in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297, which is the foundational authority for the pay-and-recover principle. Multiple judgments in the corpus (Satto, Yallavva, Chennamma, Vijayakumar) cite and apply Swaran Singh. Counsel should independently read Swaran Singh.

The corpus does not contain Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680 (Constitution Bench on quantum). The quantum framework in this report relies on Surendra Singh (doc_019) which applies Pranay Sethi, and on the compute_quantum tool which implements the Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma framework.

The corpus does not contain Magma General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Nanu Ram (2018) 18 SCC 130 or United India Insurance Co. v. Satinder Kaur (2020) 11 SCC 419 on consortium for multiple claimants. The conventional heads calculation relies on these authorities as applied by the compute_quantum tool.

doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) is a Tribunal-level decision, not a High Court or Supreme Court judgment. While factually on point, its precedential value is limited. However, it correctly applies Supreme Court principles (Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba, Shamanna v. Oriental Insurance) which are binding.

doc_028 (Sukumarbai), doc_029 (Minor Mahesh Kanubhai), doc_014 (Shivlal), and doc_026 (Ellappa) are all about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a category the Supreme Court has held is NOT covered by the statutory insurance requirement. They are entirely inapplicable to our case where the deceased was a third-party road user, not a passenger in the offending vehicle.

doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) is about a tractor used for non-agricultural purposes — a use-of-vehicle breach, not a licence breach. The legal framework for licence breaches under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) is different and governed by Swaran Singh/Satto/Yallavva which mandate pay-and-recover.

doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) is about a non-dependent legal representative (major employed son) not being entitled to loss of dependency. Our claimants are a widow and two minor children — all clearly dependants. This case is irrelevant.
doc_016 and doc_017 are criminal revision cases about rash driving convictions under IPC. They do not address civil liability, insurance, or licence breach issues and are irrelevant.

doc_023 (Suman Lata) is about reduction of interest rate from 9% to 7.5% and the insurer's inability to challenge quantum without Section 170 permission. It does not address licence breach or insurer liability.
doc_038 (Crown Consultants) is a consumer dispute about late claim filing — entirely unrelated to motor accident third-party claims.
doc_051 (Yashpal Chaudhrani) and doc_054 (Chinnasamy) are criminal quashing and specific performance cases respectively — completely unrelated to motor accident insurance.
doc_006 (Meena) focuses on contributory negligence and quantum enhancement. It does not address insurer liability for licence breach and is not adverse on the liability issue.
